idea: Largest Sidon set in {1..n} that is also sum-free

evidence: OEIS A003022 (our thresholds 1, 3, 6, 11, 17, 25, 34, 44, 55, 72 are its terms)

idea: No three in line in the triangular grid
reason: already in the OEIS

idea: Snakes (longest induced paths) in Fibonacci cubes
reason: already in the OEIS

idea: Exact sizes of corner-free sets in the n x n grid
reason: the corners problem is heavily studied

idea: Fewest monochromatic Schur triples in 3-colourings of {1..n}
reason: studied (minimum monochromatic Schur triples and generalizations)

reason: Ramsey multiplicity of cycles studied

idea: 2-colourings of grids with no monochromatic square in any orientation
reason: studied (homothetic and similar copies in square and triangular grids)

reason: Erdos's distinct subset sums problem in higher dimensions is studied

reason: studied

reason: studied

idea: Schur numbers of the Gaussian integers (sum-free colourings of Gaussian integers in a box)

idea: Largest code in the 600-cell or E8 root graph with a given graph distance
reason: closed by our own computation: a meet-in-the-middle search settled the sizes we would have posed, so nothing open remained

idea: Ising antiferromagnet on the Gosset graph (E7 polytope 3_21)
reason: closed by our own computation: a configuration meets the eigenvalue bound, so the ground state is known
evidence: our computation, 9 November 2026

idea: Largest DNA codes free of reverse complements for small lengths
reason: the simple upper bound is attained for every small length we could check, so the small cases are not open; larger lengths sit inside the studied theory of DNA codes
evidence: our computation, 9 November 2026; DNA codes with reverse-complement constraints are a studied subject

idea: Sidon sets made of quadratic residues modulo p
reason: dropped after first computations: not interesting enough as a problem of its own

reason: dropped: our first values were weak and the problem adds little to Golomb rulers

idea: Sets avoiding all solutions of a fixed Diophantine equation (anti-Diophantine sets)
reason: dropped: the extremal sets follow a trivial pattern

idea: Smallest decycling set (feedback vertex set) of the E8 root graph
reason: dropped: our first value was weak, too far from any lower bound to make a meaningful first value
evidence: our computation, 9 November 2026

idea: Ising antiferromagnet on planar point-set graphs (sunflower or Delaunay graphs)
reason: dropped: maximum cut of a planar graph is solvable in polynomial time, so these are not hard open cells
evidence: maximum cut is polynomial on planar graphs (Hadlock 1975)

idea: Ising antiferromagnet on the 120-cell
reason: closed by our own computation: a configuration meets the pentagon bound
evidence: each of the 720 pentagonal faces needs an unsatisfied edge and every edge lies in 3 faces, so E >= -1200 + 2 x 240 = -720; simulated annealing (tools/src/ising.c) reaches E = -720

idea: Domination number (covering code of radius 1) of the 120-cell graph
reason: closed by our own computation: the 120-cell graph has a perfect code
evidence: an exact-cover search finds 120 vertices whose closed neighbourhoods partition the 600 vertices, so the domination number is 600/5 = 120

idea: Ising antiferromagnet on the triangle-free strongly regular graphs (Gewirtz, M22, Higman-Sims), the graphs of the untracked tools/trianglefree_srg.py
reason: closed or too small: for the Gewirtz and Higman-Sims graphs a configuration meets the eigenvalue bound; the M22 graph has 77 vertices, within reach of exact max-cut solvers
evidence: simulated annealing (tools/src/ising.c) reaches E = -112 (Gewirtz) and -400 (Higman-Sims), the eigenvalue bounds m - n(k - lambda_min)/2; M22: -224 found against the bound -230

idea: Identifying codes of the Higman-Sims graph
reason: not added: identifying codes of vertex-transitive and strongly regular graphs are studied, and two identifying-code problems of ours exist
evidence: S. Gravier, A. Parreau, S. Rottey, L. Storme, E. Vandomme, Identifying codes in vertex-transitive graphs and strongly regular graphs (arXiv:1411.5275)

idea: Largest aluminium content of zeolite frameworks under Loewenstein's rule (independent sets of the T-site net)
reason: studied: the independence quotient of periodic nets
evidence: R. Klee (1974) and J.-G. Eon, M. Moreira de Oliveira (Acta Cryst. A, 2021), found by web search on 9 November 2026

idea: No four concyclic points in the triangular grid
reason: too close to current work on the no-four-on-a-circle problem in lattices
evidence: arXiv:2609.20447 (The extensible no-four-on-a-circle problem, 2026); OEIS A395821 (n x n grid, no four on a circle or a line)

idea: Benzenoids with the most or the fewest spanning trees
reason: dropped: spanning-tree counts of benzenoid chains and the spanning-tree density of benzenoids are studied, and by planar duality the count is det(6I - A) for the adjacency matrix A of the hexagon graph, which made the extremes look structured rather than hard
evidence: arXiv:2102.02089 (spanning trees of pyrene and triphenylene chains); Gutman, Mallion and Essam on spanning-tree density

idea: HP lattice proteins on the FCC lattice (Fibonacci sequences)
reason: dropped: HP folding on the FCC lattice is solved exactly for long sequences by hydrophobic-core construction
evidence: R. Backofen, S. Will, A constraint-based approach to fast and exact structure prediction in three-dimensional protein models, Constraints 11 (2006) 5-30 (the CPSP tools)

idea: Splitting a segmented mirror into the fewest non-redundant groups (pupil remapping by segment tilting)
reason: the question is studied; only our instance (the hexagonal segment layout with its centre removed) was new
evidence: A. K. Taras, G. Piroscia, P. Tuthill, Jewel Optics I (arXiv:2501.01570, 2025): pupils tiled by as few non-redundant sets as possible, found by local search; the Keck segment-tilting experiment (Monnier et al. 2009, arXiv:0905.3495). Our exact values (Keck's 36 segments need 5 groups, 4 are impossible) stay in our records.

idea: The slewing tour of the Bright Star Catalogue for an equatorial mount
reason: the question is studied; only our instance (the catalogue and the idealised mount metric) was new
evidence: the Traveling Telescope Problem (L. Handley, E. A. Petigura, V. V. Misic, arXiv:2310.18497) and survey schedulers that order targets by slew time as a travelling salesman problem (Zwicky Transient Facility, arXiv:1905.02209)

idea: The smallest star-tracker catalogue with at least three stars in every field of view
reason: the question is studied; only our instance (the Bright Star Catalogue with V <= 5.5, 10-degree fields, HEALPix pointings) was new
evidence: guide-star catalogue generation for star trackers: the design rule of more than two stars in every field, solved by catalogue thinning, genetic algorithms, entropy and probability criteria (e.g. Generation of guide star catalog for star trackers, IEEE Sensors Journal 2018)

idea: An optimal strategy for Primel (Wordle played on the 8,363 five-digit primes)
reason: the question is solved for Wordle-type games; a new word list is a new instance of a solved problem class, not a new question
evidence: exact optimal Wordle strategies (A. Selby 2022; D. Bertsimas and A. Paskov, Operations Research, doi:10.1287/opre.2022.0434) and Mastermind (D. E. Knuth 1976; K. Koyama and T. W. Lai 1993). Our strategy (29,016 guesses, average 3.4696; lower bound 24,866) stays in our records.
